definition.title: Scale Explorer
learning_objectives: Read characteristic size across many orders of magnitude.
Explain why a logarithmic display is useful for comparing very different sizes.
Distinguish characteristic size from distance, location, and the size of the whole universe.

input_schema.name: selected_node_id
input_schema.invalid_handling: Reject unknown, malformed, unsupported-version, and extra-field state.

relationships: Convert kilometre and light-year source values to metres in the Python astronomy model before ordering.
For radius-backed planet entries: characteristic diameter = 2 × source radius.
For direct diameter entries: characteristic diameter = source diameter.
For width and extent entries: preserve the cited characteristic quantity; do not infer a diameter.
For ratio comparisons: selected characteristic size / reference characteristic size.
For visualization only: p = 100 × (log10(S) − log10(Smin)) / (log10(Smax) − log10(Smin)).
For light-year entries: 1 ly ≈ 9.46 × 10^15 m for SI normalization, ordering, and derived ratios; this is an approximate conversion, not a new measurement.

characteristic_size.inputs: source_value, source_unit, and source_quantity in the Python astronomy model
characteristic_size.valid_domain: source_value is finite and greater than zero; source unit and quantity are supported
characteristic_size.numerical_tolerance: Deterministic floating-point checks use a relative arithmetic tolerance of 1e-12 where a tolerance is required. Source values and the 9.46 × 10^15 m/ly conversion are rounded approximations; this is not a source-uncertainty estimate.

derived_comparison.inputs: selected and reference characteristic sizes calculated by the Python astronomy model in metres
derived_comparison.valid_domain: both canonical characteristic sizes are finite and greater than zero
derived_comparison.numerical_tolerance: Deterministic floating-point checks use a relative arithmetic tolerance of 1e-12. Learner-facing comparison sentences round to two significant figures; source values remain approximate and are not assigned extra precision.

output_schema: selected node and adjacent curated nodes
source-preserving characteristic size and quantity label
definition.visualization_module: A static 2D track places each curated node by logarithmic characteristic size; it never places nodes in physical space.
assumptions: Each node uses one characteristic size chosen and labelled for that node.
Approximate or estimated source values remain approximate; no uncertainty is manufactured.
The track compares characteristic sizes only and does not model distance, nesting, or co-location.
Light-year conversion is an approximate SI normalization used for ordering and ratios, not a new measurement.
limitations: The list is curated rather than complete and has no continuous interpolation between nodes.
Planet entries use the approximate radii in the NASA Solar System Sizes reference and a definitional diameter derivation; other NASA pages may report a differently defined equatorial diameter.
The Moon keeps the directly reported 3,475 km diameter from its cited fast-facts sheet rather than deriving a diameter from a separately rounded radius.
Galaxy and observable-universe extents are broad estimates with boundary-definition limits.
The observable universe is not the same thing as the entire universe.

nodes.name: Moon
nodes.source_basis: NASA's fast-facts sheet reports a diameter of 3,475 km.

transition_explanation.text: Start with a familiar natural satellite. Its diameter is thousands of kilometres, already far beyond everyday scales.

nodes.name: Mercury
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 2,440 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: Mercury is only about one-and-a-half Moon diameters wide. A logarithmic scale keeps that modest step visible without pretending every step is equal.

derived_quantity.valid_domain: Each input canonical characteristic size is finite and greater than zero; both inputs are distinct curated nodes.
derived_quantity.numerical_tolerance: Deterministic floating-point checks use a relative arithmetic tolerance of 1e-12. The learner-facing phrase is an approximate educational rounding, not a precision claim.
derived_quantity.learner_facing_rounding: The calculated ratio is rounded to the authored phrase ‘about one-and-a-half’.

nodes.name: Mars
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 3,390 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: Mars's characteristic size is larger than Mercury's, but still below Earth's in this curated list.

nodes.name: Venus
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 6,052 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: Venus and Earth are close in characteristic size in this curated list. This size comparison alone does not model surface conditions or history.

nodes.name: Earth
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 6,371 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

comparison.text: Reference point for the planetary comparisons.

transition_explanation.text: Earth is the reference point in the planetary comparisons. The next nodes are much larger worlds, then the Sun.

nodes.comparison_text: Reference point for the planetary comparisons.

nodes.name: Neptune
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 24,622 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: The outer planets move us into tens of thousands of kilometres. Neptune is nearly four Earth characteristic diameters across by this characteristic measure.

derived_quantity.valid_domain: Each input canonical characteristic size is finite and greater than zero; both inputs are distinct curated nodes.
derived_quantity.numerical_tolerance: Deterministic floating-point checks use a relative arithmetic tolerance of 1e-12. The learner-facing phrase is an approximate educational rounding, not a precision claim.
derived_quantity.learner_facing_rounding: The calculated ratio is rounded to the authored phrase ‘nearly four’.

nodes.name: Uranus
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 25,362 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: Uranus is only slightly larger than Neptune in this list. The logarithmic view makes their small relative difference legible.

nodes.name: Saturn
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 58,232 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: Saturn takes another large step upward. Its rings are not included: this node represents the planet's listed characteristic size.

nodes.name: Jupiter
nodes.source_basis: NASA lists an approximate radius of 69,911 km; Lumina derives the characteristic diameter as 2 × radius.

transition_explanation.text: Jupiter is the largest planet in this curated set. The next node changes category: from a planet to a star.

nodes.name: Sun
nodes.source_basis: NASA describes the Sun's diameter as about 1.4 million km.

transition_explanation.text: A star is a different scale category from a planet. In this curated characteristic-size comparison, the Sun is about ten times Jupiter's characteristic diameter.

derived_quantity.valid_domain: Each input canonical characteristic size is finite and greater than zero; both inputs are distinct curated nodes.
derived_quantity.numerical_tolerance: Deterministic floating-point checks use a relative arithmetic tolerance of 1e-12. The learner-facing phrase is an approximate educational rounding, not a precision claim.
derived_quantity.learner_facing_rounding: The calculated ratio is rounded to the authored phrase ‘about ten’.

nodes.name: Milky Way galaxy
nodes.source_basis: NASA describes the Milky Way as about 100,000 light-years across; this node uses that cited galaxy-wide width as an approximate characteristic value without defining a precise boundary.

transition_explanation.text: The next category is a galaxy. Its approximate galaxy-wide width is expressed in light-years rather than kilometres; this track compares width, not physical location.

nodes.name: Observable universe
nodes.source_basis: NASA gives about 92 billion light-years across as an estimate for the observable universe; the full universe may be larger and its total size is not reliably known.

transition_explanation.text: This final node is the observable part of the universe, not a claim about the size of the entire universe. Expansion matters to the cosmological estimate.

nodes.comparison_text: About 920,000× the Milky Way galaxy's approximate width.

validation_fixtures.purpose: Independent known-case check for the directly reported Moon diameter.
Independent known-case check for the Earth reference diameter.
Independent known-case check for the rounded Sun diameter.
Independent known-case input for the large relative-comparison result.
Upper endpoint and light-year conversion edge-case check.

scientific_validation.method: Independent Python standard-library Decimal arithmetic recalculates characteristic sizes, all logarithmic display positions, and all pairwise ratios from the reviewed source_value/source_unit/source_quantity fields; results are compared with the Astropy-backed astronomy model artifact using the documented tolerance.
